prompt.context: It is 2009. Wally's Wire Factory makes electronics cables. Like most players in the industry, Wally's Wire Factory makes a large range of cables, wires, connectors, converters, and basic electronics extras. It has a steady stream of business and has little desire to expand into new products. Wally's Wire Factory has hired you to help increase profitability from its existing businesses.
prompt.question: How can Wally's Wire Factory increase profitability from its existing businesses?

clarifying_info.a: There are significant barriers to entry, so there have been no new competitors in the past 5 years, and Wally's projects it would take 2-3 years for a new competitor to enter. Competition varies significantly by region.
Wally's is the leader of an established mature industry that is growing at the rate of GDP.
There is a range of higher and lower end products, and margins vary considerably by product line.
Customers are mainly IT departments and retail businesses, but there is a sizable number of technology-minded individuals who make direct purchases as well.

exhibits.title: Wire Market Share Data, 2006
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar chart showing market share percentages for Wally's, Competitor 1, Competitor 2, and Competitor 3 across three regions: North America, Europe, and Asia, as of 2006.

exhibits.title: Wire Market Share Data, 2009
exhibits.shows: Stacked bar chart showing market share percentages for Wally's, Competitor 1, Competitor 2, and Competitor 3 across three regions: North America, Europe, and Asia, as of 2009.

exhibits.title: Gross Margin vs. X-Axis Variable (blank)
exhibits.shows: A chart template plotting gross margin by product on the y-axis. The x-axis is left for the candidate to define.

exhibits.title: Expected Pattern: Price Elasticity vs. Gross Margin
exhibits.shows: A conceptual scatter plot illustrating what pattern would be expected if price elasticity were plotted on the x-axis against gross margin, showing a downward trend hypothesis.

exhibits.title: Actual Scatter Plot: Price Elasticity vs. Gross Margin by Product
exhibits.shows: A scatter plot of Wally's products with price elasticity on the x-axis and gross margin on the y-axis, divided into four quadrants. The data shows little overall correlation between price elasticity and gross margin.

framework: Diagnose the competitive landscape across regions using market share data (2006 vs. 2009)
Identify which region offers the best opportunity to increase profitability
Investigate margin drivers within the target region — starting with product-level margin variation
Assess pricing power by analyzing price elasticity relative to gross margin by product line
Recommend differentiated pricing strategies by quadrant (raise/lower prices based on elasticity and current margin)

questions.prompt: What happened over the past three years (2006-2009) in each region?
questions.guidance: North America: Wally's share grew (52%→54%), suggesting strong buyer power or entrenched position. IT buyers with small-component costs have limited price sensitivity. Competitor 1 lost share. Europe: Wally's share dropped significantly (41%→34%); Competitor 1 grew, likely through price cuts, suggesting commoditization pressure. Asia: Competition intensified; Competitor 1 grew at Competitor 3's expense. All firms splitting profits suggests late-stage pricing parity settling in. Retail buyers (price-sensitive, expensive input) are eroding industry margins. Note: cannot infer market size growth from share data alone.

questions.prompt: In which market are we best able to increase profits from existing businesses, and how should we approach this?
questions.guidance: Europe and Asia are unlikely candidates because the product is being commoditized and price competition is intense. North America is the best opportunity: Wally's holds and is growing its leadership position, competition is less extreme, and there may be room to capture value through pricing. Within North America, margins vary by product line, so the next step is to understand what drives those variations.

questions.prompt: We want to understand North American margin variation across products. Gross margin is on the y-axis. What variable(s) might we want to plot on the x-axis?
questions.guidance: A strong answer suggests price elasticity as the x-axis variable, because without extreme competition in North America there may be room to increase profits through pricing. The candidate should also explain what data pattern would emerge and what strategic action would follow — not just name the axis. Other reasonable answers are acceptable if accompanied by a strategic rationale.

questions.prompt: If we chart price elasticity on the x-axis, what pattern would we expect, and what pattern would indicate considerable room to improve profitability?
questions.guidance: Expected pattern: products with high price elasticity should have the lowest gross margins (close substitutes, price-driven consumers); products with low price elasticity should have higher margins (differentiated features). This implies a clear downward trend. Any scatter plot that does NOT show a clear downward trend indicates that margins are not aligned with elasticity, meaning significant room exists to improve profitability through price adjustments.

questions.prompt: After plotting price elasticity vs. gross margin, the actual chart shows little correlation. What do you conclude and recommend?
questions.guidance: Lower-left quadrant (low elasticity, low margin): raise prices — demand is inelastic so volume loss will be minimal, and margin improvement will be substantial. Upper-right quadrant (high elasticity, high margin): consider cutting prices — volume gains from price reduction will outweigh margin compression, boosting revenue. Upper-left quadrant (low elasticity, high margin): current pricing is well-optimized; revenue can still be maintained or grown through price. Lower-right quadrant (high elasticity, low margin): most challenged; consider cost reduction or de-prioritization.

recommendation: Wally's is unlikely to increase profitability in Europe and Asia because its product is being commoditized in those markets
Focus profitability improvement efforts on North America, where Wally's holds a strong and growing leadership position
Since competition is less extreme in North America, there is room to increase profits through differentiated pricing
Raise prices on products with low price elasticity and currently low gross margins (lower-left quadrant)
Lower prices on products with high price elasticity and currently high gross margins (upper-right quadrant) to gain volume
risks: Misjudging elasticity estimates could lead to volume loss if prices are raised too aggressively
Competitors could respond to North American pricing moves by lowering their own prices
Commoditization pressure from Europe and Asia could eventually reach North America
next_steps: Conduct detailed product-level price elasticity analysis to validate quadrant classifications
Model revenue and margin impact of proposed price changes before implementation
Monitor European and Asian market dynamics to track whether commoditization is moving toward North America
